EXPLANATION: taskset controls CPU affinity — which CPUs a process can run on. -c 0,1 specifies CPU cores 0 and 1 by number. cpulimit limits CPU percentage usage (e.g., 50%) not specific cores. ulimit -c limits core dump file size, not CPU cores. nice adjusts scheduling priority but not CPU affinity.

QUESTION: What does 'journalctl --disk-usage' show?
OPTION_A: The rate at which journal files are growing over time
OPTION_B: The total disk space currently used by all systemd journal files
OPTION_C: Per-unit disk usage statistics for services that write to the journal
OPTION_D: Available disk space on the partition where journal files are stored
EXPLANATION: journalctl --disk-usage shows the total size of all journal files on disk (e.g., 'Archived and active journals take up X.XM in the file system.'). It does not break down by service/unit. Available space is shown by df. Growth rate requires comparing multiple measurements over time.

QUESTION: Which command correctly configures a static IP address 192.168.1.100/24 with gateway 192.168.1.1 on interface eth0 using NetworkManager?
OPTION_A: nmcli set eth0 ip=192.168.1.100/24 gw=192.168.1.1 static && nmcli restart eth0
OPTION_C: networkctl eth0 static 192.168.1.100/24 via 192.168.1.1 && networkctl reload
OPTION_D: nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.100/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 ipv4.method manual && nmcli con up eth0
EXPLANATION: nmcli con mod modifies a connection profile. ipv4.addresses sets the address, ipv4.gateway the gateway, ipv4.method manual disables DHCP. Then nmcli con up activates the changes. nmcli set is not valid syntax. networkctl is systemd-networkd's tool (different network manager). nmtui is an interactive TUI, not a command-line configuration tool.

QUESTION: What does 'rpm -Uvh package.rpm' do on a RHEL system?
OPTION_A: Upgrades the package if installed or installs it fresh with verbose output and progress hash marks
OPTION_B: Verifies the package signature and hash then installs only if verification passes
OPTION_C: Uninstalls the current version then reinstalls the package from the local rpm file
OPTION_D: Updates only the package database hash without installing the package binaries
EXPLANATION: -U upgrades (or installs if not present), -v verbose, -h hash marks progress. rpm -V (verify) checks installed packages. Signature verification uses -K. rpm does not uninstall then reinstall — it upgrades in place preserving config files. The 'h' is hash (progress), not hash verification.

QUESTION: Which file format does 'dpkg --get-selections' output and what is it used for?
OPTION_A: Generates a binary database file compatible with apt cache for offline package installation
OPTION_B: Outputs a list of all installed packages with their selection state used to recreate the package installation on another system with dpkg --set-selections
OPTION_C: Produces a list of manually installed packages excluding automatically installed dependencies
OPTION_D: Creates an XML manifest of installed packages for compliance auditing and reporting
EXPLANATION: dpkg --get-selections outputs 'package	install' lines that can be piped or saved, then used on another system with 'dpkg --set-selections < list' followed by 'apt-get dselect-upgrade' to install the same packages. It is plain text, not binary or XML. It includes all packages (not just manually installed ones — use apt-mark showmanual for that).

QUESTION: What is the effect of adding 'vm.swappiness=10' to /etc/sysctl.conf?
OPTION_A: Forces the kernel to swap 10MB of memory per minute for memory maintenance
OPTION_B: Configures 10 swap partitions to be used simultaneously for parallel swap operations
OPTION_C: Sets the swap partition size to 10% of total RAM regardless of physical swap space available
OPTION_D: Reduces the kernel's tendency to swap memory to disk preferring to keep data in RAM until RAM is nearly full
EXPLANATION: vm.swappiness controls how aggressively the kernel swaps. 0 = avoid swapping (swap only when out of memory), 60 = default, 100 = swap aggressively. Setting to 10 means the kernel strongly prefers RAM and only swaps under significant memory pressure. It does not set swap size, define swap rates in MB, or configure multiple swap devices.

QUESTION: Which command shows the complete routing table including IPv6 routes?
OPTION_A: ip route show && ip -6 route show
OPTION_B: netstat -rn6
OPTION_C: routetable --all --ipv6
OPTION_D: route -A inet6
EXPLANATION: 'ip route show' shows IPv4 routes. 'ip -6 route show' (or 'ip route show table all' for all tables) shows IPv6 routes. netstat -rn shows routing table but netstat -rn6 may not work on all systems (deprecated). 'route -A inet6' works on some older systems but ip is the modern tool. routetable is not a Linux command.

QUESTION: What does 'ldconfig' do and when should it be run?
OPTION_A: Lists all dynamically linked libraries required by currently running processes
OPTION_B: Updates the dynamic linker run-time bindings cache after installing new shared libraries
OPTION_C: Reloads the PAM configuration for LDAP authentication services
OPTION_D: Compiles and links a custom kernel module into the running kernel
EXPLANATION: ldconfig scans /etc/ld.so.conf and standard library directories, then updates /etc/ld.so.cache so the dynamic linker finds shared libraries efficiently. Run after installing or updating shared libraries (.so files) or when /etc/ld.so.conf is changed. ldd lists dependencies of a binary. Kernel modules use modprobe/insmod. PAM LDAP uses nsswitch.conf and pam_ldap.

QUESTION: An administrator needs to see all kernel modules currently loaded and their dependencies. Which command provides this?
OPTION_A: lsmod
OPTION_B: modprobe --list
OPTION_C: modules --show-loaded
OPTION_D: depmod -n
EXPLANATION: lsmod reads /proc/modules and displays all currently loaded kernel modules with their size and use count (and what modules use them). modprobe --list is not valid (use modprobe -l but it lists available, not loaded). depmod generates dependency files (modules.dep). 'modules --show-loaded' is not a valid command.

QUESTION: What does 'ss -s' output?
OPTION_A: A list of all sockets sorted by state showing only established connections
OPTION_B: The per-interface socket statistics including send and receive queue sizes
OPTION_C: A summary of SSL/TLS secured connections currently established on the system
OPTION_D: A summary of socket statistics showing total counts of TCP UDP RAW and other socket states
EXPLANATION: ss -s (summary) displays aggregate statistics: total sockets, TCP connections in various states (ESTAB, LISTEN, CLOSE-WAIT, etc.), UDP, RAW counts. It does not list individual sockets. It is not per-interface. SSL/TLS is an application layer concept — ss works at the socket/transport layer.

QUESTION: Which /proc file shows the command line used to start a process with PID 1234?
OPTION_A: /proc/1234/status
OPTION_B: /proc/1234/cmdline
OPTION_C: /proc/1234/comm
OPTION_D: /proc/1234/exe
EXPLANATION: /proc/PID/cmdline contains the complete command line of the process (null-separated arguments). /proc/PID/exe is a symlink to the executable binary. /proc/PID/comm contains only the short process name (up to 15 chars). /proc/PID/status shows the process status including name, state, PID, memory usage.

QUESTION: A system administrator needs to set up log rotation for /var/log/myapp.log to rotate weekly keeping 4 weeks of logs and compressing old files. What /etc/logrotate.d/myapp configuration achieves this?
OPTION_A: /var/log/myapp.log { weekly rotate 4 compress delaycompress missingok notifempty }
OPTION_B: /var/log/myapp.log { schedule weekly retain 4 compress }
OPTION_C: rotate /var/log/myapp.log --weekly --keep=4 --gzip
OPTION_D: /var/log/myapp.log { interval=weekly count=4 compress=yes }
EXPLANATION: logrotate.d syntax uses a block format: filename { directives }. weekly sets rotation frequency, rotate 4 keeps 4 files, compress enables compression, delaycompress delays compression by one cycle (so the current rotated file isn't compressed yet, allowing running processes to still write), missingok doesn't error if file is missing, notifempty skips empty files. The other options use invalid logrotate syntax.

QUESTION: Which command shows detailed NUMA topology and memory statistics on a NUMA system?
OPTION_A: lscpu --numa
OPTION_B: numactl --hardware
OPTION_C: lstopo --numa-memory
OPTION_D: numastats --topology
EXPLANATION: numactl --hardware (or numactl -H) displays NUMA node topology, memory per node, and node distances. numastats is not a standard command. lscpu --numa is not valid (lscpu shows CPU topology but not NUMA memory stats; use 'lscpu' with no flag to see NUMA information). lstopo is from hwloc package and shows hardware topology but --numa-memory is not a valid option.

QUESTION: What does 'update-alternatives --config java' do on a Debian/Ubuntu system?
OPTION_A: Updates the Java package to the latest version available in the repository
OPTION_B: Configures Java security settings and trusted certificate authorities
OPTION_C: Automatically selects the newest installed Java version as the system default
OPTION_D: Presents an interactive menu to select which installed JVM should be the default java command
EXPLANATION: update-alternatives manages symlinks for commands with multiple versions. --config java shows installed java alternatives and prompts the administrator to select the default. It does not automatically select any version (that is --auto). It does not update packages (use apt). It does not configure security settings.

QUESTION: What is the difference between 'kill -9 PID' and 'kill -15 PID'?
OPTION_A: Kill -9 terminates the process and removes its core dump while kill -15 keeps the core for debugging
OPTION_B: Signal 9 kills only the specified process while signal 15 kills the entire process group including children
OPTION_C: Signal 15 (SIGTERM) asks the process to terminate gracefully allowing cleanup while signal 9 (SIGKILL) forcibly terminates the process immediately with no cleanup possible
OPTION_D: Signal 15 works on all processes while signal 9 requires root privileges to send
EXPLANATION: SIGTERM (15): polite request to terminate — the process can catch this signal, clean up resources, save state, then exit. SIGKILL (9): cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored — kernel forcibly removes the process immediately with no cleanup. Both signals can be sent to processes the sender owns or (as root) to any process. Neither selectively kills process groups (use kill -15 -PID for group). Neither creates or removes core dumps.

QUESTION: Which command exports an environment variable so it is available to child processes?
OPTION_A: export MYVAR=value
OPTION_B: env MYVAR=value persist
OPTION_C: MYVAR=value && expose MYVAR
OPTION_D: set -x MYVAR=value
EXPLANATION: export marks a variable for inheritance by child processes (subshells, commands). Without export, the variable is local to the current shell. 'expose' is not a bash command. 'set -x' enables debug mode. 'env MYVAR=value command' sets it for one command only but doesn't persist in the shell.

QUESTION: An administrator runs 'strace -p 1234' on a running process. What does this show?
OPTION_A: The open file descriptors and network connections belonging to the process
OPTION_B: All library functions called by the process using its dynamic link libraries
OPTION_C: The process memory map showing all virtual memory regions and their permissions
OPTION_D: All system calls made by the process in real time including arguments and return values
EXPLANATION: strace traces system calls (kernel interface calls like read, write, open, socket, execve). -p attaches to a running process. It shows each syscall with arguments and return value. Memory map is from /proc/PID/maps or pmap. Library calls (not syscalls) require ltrace. Open files and connections use lsof.

QUESTION: What does 'sar -u 1 5' report?
OPTION_A: Memory usage statistics sampled once per 5 seconds for 1 minute
OPTION_B: CPU utilization statistics updated every 1 second for 5 intervals
OPTION_C: Network interface utilization for the last 5 hours updated hourly
OPTION_D: Disk I/O statistics for 5 seconds collected once per minute
EXPLANATION: sar (System Activity Reporter): -u reports CPU utilization, 1 is the interval in seconds, 5 is the count. So: 5 samples of CPU stats, one per second. The syntax is 'sar [options] [interval [count]]'. Memory would be sar -r. Disk I/O is sar -d. Network is sar -n DEV.

QUESTION: Which command displays the default gateway configured on the system?
OPTION_A: ip route show default
OPTION_B: gateway --show
OPTION_C: netstat --default-gw
OPTION_D: route --gateway
EXPLANATION: 'ip route show default' filters the routing table to show only the default route (0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0) which contains the gateway IP. 'route --gateway' is not valid syntax. 'netstat --default-gw' is not valid. 'gateway --show' is not a Linux command. You can also use 'ip route | grep default'.

QUESTION: What does the 'chroot' command do?
OPTION_A: Changes the ownership of the root directory / to a specified user for maintenance operations
OPTION_B: Restricts the root user to a specific terminal or console for security purposes
OPTION_C: Creates a new root user account on the system with a custom home directory path
OPTION_D: Changes the root directory for the current process and its children creating an isolated filesystem environment
EXPLANATION: chroot changes the apparent root directory (/). Everything above the new root is invisible to the chrooted process. Used for: system repair (boot from live media, chroot into broken system), building packages in isolation, and basic container-like environments (though less secure than modern containers). It does not change ownership, restrict root logins, or create accounts.

QUESTION: A system is running slow and 'top' shows high 'wa' percentage. What does 'wa' represent?
OPTION_A: The number of processes in wait state blocked on system calls
OPTION_B: The percentage of CPU time spent waiting for I/O operations to complete
OPTION_C: The percentage of memory allocated to write-ahead logging buffers
OPTION_D: The total wall clock time elapsed since the system last rebooted
EXPLANATION: In top/vmstat, 'wa' (or %wa) is I/O wait — CPU time where the CPU is idle but waiting for disk or network I/O. High wa% indicates an I/O bottleneck. It is not uptime (that is the top header or uptime command). It is not a memory metric. Process count in wait state is visible in the process list with D state.

QUESTION: Which command adds the repository public key to apt's trusted keys on Ubuntu?
OPTION_A: wget -O - https://repo.example.com/key.gpg | sudo apt-key add -
OPTION_B: gpg --import key.gpg && sudo apt-key update
OPTION_C: curl -fsSL https://repo.example.com/key.gpg | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/repo.gpg
OPTION_D: apt-key add https://repo.example.com/key.gpg
EXPLANATION: The modern method (Ubuntu 20.04+): download key with curl, dearmor and place in /usr/share/keyrings/. Then reference in sources.list with 'signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/repo.gpg'. apt-key is deprecated. 'gpg --import' imports to user GPG keyring not apt trusted keys. 'wget | apt-key add -' worked previously but apt-key is deprecated in modern Ubuntu.

QUESTION: What does 'systemd-analyze blame' output?
OPTION_A: Lists all service units sorted by the time they took to start during the last boot from slowest to fastest
OPTION_B: Identifies units that are improperly configured and may cause security vulnerabilities
OPTION_C: Displays who last modified each systemd unit file and when the changes were made
OPTION_D: Shows which systemd units failed during boot with their error messages and exit codes
EXPLANATION: systemd-analyze blame: shows startup time for each unit sorted by longest first. Helps identify what is slowing down boot. Failed units are shown by 'systemctl --failed'. Unit file modification history would use git or rpm/dpkg. Security analysis is done by separate tools.

QUESTION: Which command creates a compressed tar archive of /etc and saves it to /backup/etc_backup.tar.gz?
OPTION_A: tar xzf /backup/etc_backup.tar.gz /etc
OPTION_B: tar czf /backup/etc_backup.tar.gz /etc
OPTION_C: tar -create -zip /backup/etc_backup.tar.gz /etc
OPTION_D: compress /etc -output /backup/etc_backup.tar.gz
EXPLANATION: tar: c=create, z=compress with gzip, f=filename. The archive is written first, then the source path. '-create -zip' are not valid tar flags. 'compress' is the older Unix compress tool, not tar. tar x=extract (opposite of create).

QUESTION: What is the purpose of the /var/spool/cron/crontabs/ directory?
OPTION_A: Contains log files of all cron job executions with their output and exit status
OPTION_B: Stores incoming mail messages from cron job output before delivery to user mailboxes
OPTION_C: Holds templates for generating user-specific cron configurations during account creation
OPTION_D: Stores individual user crontab files managed by the cron daemon for scheduled job execution
EXPLANATION: /var/spool/cron/crontabs/ (or /var/spool/cron/ on some systems) contains one file per user with that user's crontab entries. These are managed by crontab command, not edited directly. Cron output logs go to syslog or /var/log/cron. Account templates are in /etc/skel/. Cron mail output goes to /var/spool/mail/ or /var/mail/.

QUESTION: What command verifies the integrity of installed RPM packages against their metadata?
OPTION_A: rpmcheck -a --verify
OPTION_B: yum verify-all
OPTION_C: rpm --integrity --all
OPTION_D: rpm -Va
EXPLANATION: rpm -Va (verify all) checks all installed packages: file sizes, checksums, permissions, ownership, and timestamps against the RPM database. It reports any discrepancies (S=size, M=mode, 5=MD5/SHA, etc.). rpm --integrity is not valid syntax. yum/dnf verify is a plugin (dnf verify), not built-in. rpmcheck is not a standard command.

QUESTION: Which command shows which services are enabled to start at boot in systemd?
OPTION_A: service --list-boot
OPTION_B: chkconfig --list --enabled
OPTION_C: systemctl show --boot-enabled
OPTION_D: systemctl list-unit-files --type=service --state=enabled
EXPLANATION: systemctl list-unit-files --type=service filters to service units; --state=enabled shows only enabled ones. 'systemctl show --boot-enabled' is not valid. chkconfig is for SysV init (deprecated on systemd systems). 'service --list-boot' is not a valid command.

QUESTION: What does 'ssh-copy-id user@remotehost' accomplish?
OPTION_A: Synchronizes SSH configuration files between the local system and the remote host
OPTION_B: Generates a new SSH key pair and installs the private key on the remote host
OPTION_C: Copies the local user's public key to the remote host's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file enabling key-based authentication
OPTION_D: Copies the remote host's host key to the local known_hosts file for host verification
EXPLANATION: ssh-copy-id appends the local ~/.ssh/id_*.pub (or specified key) to the remote user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. After this, the user can SSH without a password using their private key. Host keys go into known_hosts during first connection. It copies the PUBLIC key (not private). It doesn't sync config files.

QUESTION: Which command shows the current SELinux mode and whether SELinux policy is loaded?
OPTION_A: getenforce
OPTION_B: seinfo --status
OPTION_C: selinux --status
OPTION_D: sestatus
EXPLANATION: sestatus shows comprehensive SELinux status: current mode, mode from config file, policy loaded, policy version, MLS/MCS status. getenforce only shows the enforcement mode (Enforcing/Permissive/Disabled) — a subset of sestatus. seinfo queries policy information but not runtime status. 'selinux --status' is not a valid command.

QUESTION: What does 'ufw allow 22/tcp' do on Ubuntu?
OPTION_A: Configures OpenSSH to accept connections on port 22 overriding sshd_config settings
OPTION_B: Adds a firewall rule to the Uncomplicated Firewall allowing incoming TCP connections on port 22
OPTION_C: Allows outbound TCP connections from the system on port 22 for SSH client connections
OPTION_D: Creates an unlimited connection window allowing any number of SSH connections from any source
EXPLANATION: ufw (Uncomplicated Firewall) is a frontend for iptables/nftables. 'allow 22/tcp' adds an ALLOW rule for incoming TCP port 22 (SSH). It does not configure sshd_config. By default ufw rules apply to incoming traffic unless 'out' is specified. Connection limits use 'ufw limit 22/tcp'.

QUESTION: An administrator wants to require SSH public key authentication and disable all password-based authentication. Which sshd_config settings are required?
OPTION_A: KeyAuthentication required AND PasswordAuth denied
OPTION_B: AuthenticationMethods publickey AND PasswordAuthentication disabled
OPTION_C: RequirePublicKey yes AND AllowPassword no
OPTION_D: PubkeyAuthentication yes AND PasswordAuthentication no AND ChallengeResponseAuthentication no
EXPLANATION: The exact sshd_config directives: PubkeyAuthentication yes (enables key auth), PasswordAuthentication no (disables password), ChallengeResponseAuthentication no (disables keyboard-interactive which can also allow passwords). AuthenticationMethods is valid but 'disabled' is not a valid value (use 'no'). RequirePublicKey, AllowPassword, KeyAuthentication, and PasswordAuth are not valid sshd_config directives.

QUESTION: What is the purpose of 'sudo visudo' versus directly editing /etc/sudoers?
OPTION_A: visudo is only required when adding new users while direct editing is acceptable for modifying existing rules
OPTION_B: visudo creates a backup of the current sudoers file before applying any changes
OPTION_C: visudo locks the file during editing and validates syntax before saving preventing a broken sudoers that could lock out all sudo access
OPTION_D: visudo encrypts the sudoers file with the root password to prevent unauthorized viewing
EXPLANATION: visudo uses the editor defined by EDITOR/VISUAL but critically: (1) locks /etc/sudoers preventing concurrent edits, (2) validates syntax before writing — if invalid, it warns and lets you re-edit. A broken /etc/sudoers with direct editing can prevent ALL sudo access including fixing the file. It does not encrypt or automatically backup. visudo should always be used for any sudoers change.

QUESTION: Which command shows which files have the SUID bit set across the entire filesystem?
OPTION_A: ls -lR / | grep '^-rws'
OPTION_B: find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
OPTION_C: find / -mode u+s -type f 2>/dev/null
OPTION_D: locate --suid / 2>/dev/null
EXPLANATION: find -perm -4000: the leading minus means 'at least these permission bits set' and 4000 is the SUID bit. -type f limits to regular files. 2>/dev/null suppresses permission errors. ls -lR / would work but generates enormous output and grep may miss some formats. '-mode u+s' is not valid find syntax (use -perm /4000 or -perm -4000). locate doesn't filter by permissions.

QUESTION: What does 'openssl s_client -connect example.com:443' accomplish?
OPTION_A: Generates a self-signed SSL certificate for example.com valid for 443 days
OPTION_B: Creates an encrypted tunnel to example.com on port 443 for secure client communication
OPTION_C: Scans example.com for SSL vulnerabilities and weak cipher suites
OPTION_D: Establishes a test TLS connection to example.com port 443 displaying certificate chain and negotiated cipher
EXPLANATION: openssl s_client -connect is a diagnostic TLS client: it connects, shows the full certificate chain, cipher suite, TLS version, and allows interactive testing. It does not generate certificates (use openssl req/x509). It does not scan for vulnerabilities (use testssl.sh or sslscan). It is a test/diagnostic tool, not a production tunnel.

QUESTION: What is the purpose of the /etc/pam.d/sshd file?
OPTION_A: Stores the SSH daemon's private host key used for server authentication to clients
OPTION_B: Configures the PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) stack used by the SSH daemon for authentication
OPTION_C: Contains the SSH client configuration applied when root connects via SSH
OPTION_D: Defines which users are permitted to use SSH based on group membership
EXPLANATION: /etc/pam.d/sshd configures PAM modules for sshd: which modules handle authentication (pam_unix, pam_ldap), account checks (pam_access), session setup (pam_limits), and password changes. SSH host keys are in /etc/ssh/. User access control is in sshd_config AllowUsers/AllowGroups. Client config is ~/.ssh/config or /etc/ssh/ssh_config.

QUESTION: Which tool provides a framework for mandatory access control on Linux using type enforcement policies separate from SELinux?
OPTION_A: grsecurity
OPTION_B: seccomp
OPTION_C: AppArmor
OPTION_D: Tomoyo
EXPLANATION: AppArmor is a MAC framework using profile-based path enforcement (common on Ubuntu/SUSE). SELinux uses type enforcement with labels. Tomoyo also provides MAC but is less common. grsecurity is a kernel patch set for hardening (commercial). seccomp (secure computing mode) restricts which system calls a process can make but is not a full MAC framework.

QUESTION: What does 'nmap -sS -O 192.168.1.0/24' do?
OPTION_A: Performs a stealthy SYN scan and OS detection on all hosts in the 192.168.1.0/24 subnet
OPTION_B: Sends ICMP echo requests to discover live hosts in the subnet without port scanning
OPTION_C: Performs a full TCP connect scan with service version detection on the subnet
OPTION_D: Scans for open UDP services and performs OS fingerprinting on the entire subnet
EXPLANATION: -sS is SYN stealth scan (half-open: sends SYN, reads response, doesn't complete handshake). -O enables OS detection (requires root). The target is the entire /24 subnet. ICMP-only discovery is -sn (ping scan). Full TCP connect is -sT. UDP scanning is -sU.

QUESTION: Which command creates a new GPG key pair interactively?
OPTION_A: openssl genrsa | gpg --import
OPTION_B: gpg-keygen --new-key
OPTION_C: gpg --full-generate-key
OPTION_D: gpg --create-key --interactive
EXPLANATION: gpg --full-generate-key (or --gen-key for quick defaults) starts an interactive dialog to create a new key pair. --create-key is not a valid gpg option. openssl genrsa creates RSA keys in PEM format, not GPG format. gpg-keygen is not a valid command.

QUESTION: What does 'tripwire --check' do?
OPTION_A: Compares the current filesystem state against a baseline database to detect unauthorized modifications
OPTION_B: Performs a connectivity test to the tripwire management server for enterprise reporting
OPTION_C: Checks the tripwire configuration file for syntax errors before initializing the database
OPTION_D: Verifies that all tripwire policy rules have matching files on the filesystem
EXPLANATION: Tripwire is a file integrity monitoring tool. --check compares current files against the baseline database (created with --init) and reports any changes in size, permissions, checksums, ownership. Syntax checking is done differently. Policy verification is a separate function. Enterprise reporting uses different tripwire commands.

QUESTION: What is the effect of 'echo 0 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/icmp_echo_ignore_all'?
OPTION_A: Enables the system to respond to ICMP echo requests (ping) if it was previously set to ignore them
OPTION_B: Configures the system to ignore all ICMP messages including redirects and unreachables
OPTION_C: Resets the ICMP rate limiting counter to zero allowing maximum ICMP traffic
OPTION_D: Disables ping responses making the system invisible to ICMP-based network discovery
EXPLANATION: icmp_echo_ignore_all=1 ignores all ICMP echo requests (disables ping). icmp_echo_ignore_all=0 enables ping responses (the default). Setting to 0 RE-ENABLES ping. To disable ping, set to 1. Setting to 0 does not affect rate limiting. ICMP redirects are controlled by accept_redirects, not this parameter.

QUESTION: Which command generates a certificate signing request (CSR) for a web server using an existing private key?
OPTION_A: openssl req -new -key server.key -out server.csr
OPTION_B: openssl gencsr --key server.key --output server.csr
OPTION_C: openssl ca -new -key server.key -out server.csr
OPTION_D: openssl x509 -signreq -in server.key -out server.csr
EXPLANATION: openssl req -new creates a CSR. -key specifies the existing private key. -out names the output CSR file. The CSR is sent to a CA for signing. openssl ca is used by a CA to sign CSRs, not create them. openssl gencsr is not a valid subcommand. openssl x509 manages certificates, not CSR creation.

QUESTION: What is 'sudoreplay' used for?
OPTION_A: Re-executes all failed sudo commands from the audit log with elevated debugging
OPTION_B: Generates a report of all sudo commands executed in the past week
OPTION_C: Replays recorded sudo session logs that were captured with the iolog_dir sudoers option
OPTION_D: Replays the last sudo command executed by a specific user for auditing purposes
EXPLANATION: sudoreplay plays back I/O logs captured by sudo when iolog_dir is configured in sudoers. This records all input/output from privileged sessions and allows exact replay for auditing. It does not replay arbitrary last commands or re-execute failed commands. Reports are generated with 'sudo -l' or external log analysis tools.

QUESTION: What does 'logwatch' do?
OPTION_A: Analyzes system log files and sends a daily digest email summarizing notable events and potential security issues
OPTION_B: Compresses and archives log files based on configured rotation schedules
OPTION_C: Forwards log entries to a remote syslog server for centralized log management
OPTION_D: Continuously monitors log files in real time and alerts on specific patterns immediately
EXPLANATION: logwatch is a log analysis tool that runs daily (typically via cron), parses various log files, and sends a summary report. It is NOT real-time (that's tools like ossec or fail2ban). Log rotation is logrotate's job. Log forwarding uses rsyslog or syslog-ng.

QUESTION: Which command shows active failed login attempts in real time from /var/log/auth.log?
OPTION_A: lastb -f /var/log/auth.log --follow
OPTION_B: authlog --monitor --failed
OPTION_C: journalctl -f -u ssh --state=failed
OPTION_D: tail -f /var/log/auth.log | grep -i 'failed\|invalid'
EXPLANATION: tail -f follows the file in real time; grep filters for failure patterns. lastb shows failed logins from /var/log/btmp but doesn't have --follow. authlog is not a standard command. journalctl -f -u ssh shows SSH journal entries in real time but --state=failed is not valid journalctl syntax.

QUESTION: What is the purpose of the 'syslog' facility in rsyslog/syslog-ng configuration?
OPTION_A: A special log file that captures all system log messages regardless of priority level
OPTION_B: A logging facility identifier used to categorize log messages by source such as kern mail auth daemon and local0-7
OPTION_C: The network protocol used to transmit log messages between systems over UDP or TCP
OPTION_D: The name of the main syslog service daemon that receives and distributes log messages
EXPLANATION: In syslog, 'facility' categorizes the source of messages: kern (kernel), mail, auth, daemon, lpr, user, local0-local7, etc. Combined with severity (emergency, alert, critical, error, warning, notice, info, debug) to create a selector. The syslog daemon is rsyslogd or syslog-ng. The protocol is also called syslog (RFC 5424/3164).

QUESTION: What does 'semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080' accomplish?
OPTION_A: Creates a new SELinux port label type called http_port_t for use on port 8080
OPTION_B: Removes the restriction on port 8080 by adding it to the unrestricted SELinux port list
OPTION_C: Adds TCP port 8080 to the http_port_t SELinux type allowing web server processes to bind to that port
OPTION_D: Modifies the system firewall to allow HTTP traffic on port 8080 with SELinux enforcement
EXPLANATION: semanage port -a (add) -t type -p protocol port: adds the port to an existing SELinux type's allowed ports. Without this, a web server configured to use port 8080 would be denied by SELinux even if Unix permissions and firewall allow it. It does not create new types (they are predefined). It does not modify iptables/firewalld. The port is added to an existing type, not made unrestricted.

QUESTION: Which command scans a local file for malware using ClamAV?
OPTION_A: clamd /path/to/scan --detect
OPTION_B: clamav --scan /path/to/scan
OPTION_C: freshclam --scan /path/to/scan
OPTION_D: clamscan -r /path/to/scan
EXPLANATION: clamscan is the ClamAV command-line scanner. -r enables recursive scanning of directories. clamav is not a command. freshclam updates the ClamAV virus database (does not scan). clamd is the daemon; it receives scan requests from clamdscan (not direct file arguments with --detect).

QUESTION: What does 'iptables -A INPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT' accomplish?
OPTION_A: Creates a stateful firewall rule that tracks connection state for outbound traffic monitoring
OPTION_B: Allows incoming packets that are part of already established connections or related to tracked connections such as FTP data channels
OPTION_C: Permits all packets with TCP flags set to ESTABLISHED from any source to any destination
OPTION_D: Blocks new incoming connections while allowing packets flagged as established to pass through
EXPLANATION: This rule uses the conntrack state module (-m state --state). ESTABLISHED means the packet belongs to an existing connection. RELATED means it's associated with an existing connection (e.g., FTP data channel related to FTP control). This allows return traffic for connections initiated from this host. It's not a TCP flag rule. It allows RELATED too. It applies to INPUT (incoming), not outbound.

QUESTION: What is the purpose of 'AIDE' (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment)?
OPTION_A: Automatically patches known vulnerabilities discovered during regular system scans
OPTION_B: Creates a database of file hashes and attributes then detects changes to monitored files indicating potential intrusion
OPTION_C: Monitors network connections in real time and blocks intrusion attempts based on signatures
OPTION_D: Provides behavioral analysis of running processes to detect malware based on system call patterns
EXPLANATION: AIDE is a file integrity monitoring tool: it builds a database of file checksums, permissions, timestamps, and other attributes, then compares current state against the database to detect unauthorized changes. This is host-based integrity monitoring, not network IDS (that's Snort/Suricata). It does not patch vulnerabilities or monitor system calls.

QUESTION: What does 'docker exec -it container_name bash' do?
OPTION_A: Opens an interactive bash shell inside a running container
OPTION_B: Starts a stopped container named container_name with bash as the entry point
OPTION_C: Creates a new container from the container_name image and runs bash in it
OPTION_D: Executes a bash script from the host filesystem inside the container
EXPLANATION: docker exec runs a command in an ALREADY RUNNING container. -i is interactive (keeps stdin open), -t allocates a pseudo-TTY. 'docker run' would create a NEW container. docker exec does not run host scripts inside containers (use volumes or COPY). 'docker start' starts stopped containers (but the exec command doesn't start stopped containers).

QUESTION: In bash, what is the difference between '>' and '>>' for output redirection?
OPTION_A: '>' overwrites the file while '>>' appends to the end of the file without removing existing content
OPTION_B: '>' redirects both stdout and stderr while '>>' redirects only stdout
OPTION_C: '>>' creates the file if it doesn't exist while '>' only redirects to existing files
OPTION_D: '>>' is a heredoc operator while '>' is the standard output redirect operator
EXPLANATION: > truncates the file to zero and writes new content (or creates the file). >> appends to existing content (or creates the file). Both create files if they don't exist. Both redirect only stdout by default (use 2> for stderr). Heredoc is << not >>.

QUESTION: What does '${VAR:-default}' do in bash parameter expansion?
OPTION_A: Returns the value of VAR if it is set and non-empty otherwise returns 'default'
OPTION_B: Sets VAR to 'default' permanently if VAR is currently unset or empty
OPTION_C: Returns 'default' only if VAR is completely unset but uses VAR's value if VAR is empty
OPTION_D: Removes the string 'default' from the end of the variable VAR's value
EXPLANATION: ${VAR:-default}: if VAR is unset OR empty, expand to 'default'; otherwise expand to $VAR. Does NOT set the variable. ${VAR:=default} SETS the variable (side effect). ${VAR-default} (without colon) only uses default if VAR is UNSET (not if empty). ${VAR%default} removes suffix 'default' from VAR.

QUESTION: What is the correct way to iterate over lines in a file using bash?
OPTION_A: read -a lines file.txt; for line in "${lines[@]}"; do echo $line; done
OPTION_B: foreach line in $(cat file.txt); do echo $line; done
OPTION_C: while IFS= read -r line; do echo "$line"; done < file.txt
OPTION_D: for line in file.txt; do echo $line; done
EXPLANATION: while IFS= read -r line: IFS= prevents leading/trailing whitespace stripping, -r prevents backslash interpretation, reads one line at a time. for line in file.txt iterates over the filename string, not file contents. foreach is csh syntax. read -a reads into an array from stdin but the syntax shown is wrong (needs < file.txt).

QUESTION: What does 'Dockerfile COPY . /app' do?
OPTION_A: Copies files from the container's /app directory to the local build context for inspection
OPTION_B: Mounts the current directory as a volume at /app when the container starts running
OPTION_C: Copies all files from the current build context directory into the /app directory inside the image
OPTION_D: Syncs changes made to the build context directory to /app in real time during container execution
EXPLANATION: COPY in Dockerfile: source is relative to the build context (directory passed to docker build), destination is inside the image. It copies AT BUILD TIME — not at runtime. VOLUME creates runtime mounts. There is no real-time sync (that's bind mounts with docker run -v). COPY is one-way: context to image.

QUESTION: Which ansible module is used to ensure a package is installed on managed hosts?
OPTION_A: ansible.builtin.package or ansible.builtin.yum/apt depending on the OS
OPTION_B: ansible.builtin.command with 'yum install' or 'apt-get install' arguments
OPTION_C: ansible.builtin.service with enabled=yes to ensure the package service runs
OPTION_D: ansible.builtin.install with name and state parameters
EXPLANATION: ansible.builtin.package is the generic package module that works across distros. ansible.builtin.yum and ansible.builtin.apt are distro-specific equivalents. Using 'command' with package managers works but is not idempotent (Ansible won't know if the package is already installed). 'install' is not an Ansible module. 'service' manages services, not package installation.

QUESTION: What does '#!/usr/bin/env python3' at the top of a script do?
OPTION_A: Sets the default Python version for all subsequent python commands in the current shell session
OPTION_B: Specifies that the script requires Python 3 but falls back to Python 2 if Python 3 is not available
OPTION_C: Uses env to find and run python3 from PATH making the script portable across systems with different Python install locations
OPTION_D: Imports the env module from Python's standard library for environment variable handling
EXPLANATION: #!/usr/bin/env python3 is a shebang line. env searches PATH for python3, so the script works even if python3 is in /usr/local/bin, /opt/python/bin, etc. rather than /usr/bin/python3. It does not affect the shell session. env is a Unix command, not a Python module. There is no fallback — if python3 is not found, the script fails.

QUESTION: In a Kubernetes deployment YAML, what does 'replicas: 3' specify?
OPTION_A: The desired number of pod instances that should be running at all times
OPTION_B: The number of container restarts allowed before the pod is marked as failed
OPTION_C: The number of Kubernetes nodes required to schedule this deployment successfully
OPTION_D: The maximum number of pods allowed during a rolling update deployment
EXPLANATION: replicas: 3 in a Deployment spec means the ReplicaSet controller maintains exactly 3 running pod instances. If one dies, a new one is created. maxSurge/maxUnavailable control rolling update pod counts. Node requirements are set by nodeSelector/affinity. Restart limits are controlled by restartPolicy and backoffLimit.

QUESTION: What does 'set -o pipefail' do in a bash script?
OPTION_A: Enables error handling so any failed command in a pipe causes immediate script exit
OPTION_B: Forces all pipe operators to use full buffering for improved performance
OPTION_C: Sets the pipeline to use named pipes (FIFOs) instead of anonymous pipes automatically
OPTION_D: Causes the pipeline to return the exit status of the rightmost command that failed rather than always returning the last command's status
EXPLANATION: Without pipefail: 'false | true' returns 0 (true's status). With set -o pipefail: 'false | true' returns 1 (false's status). This is critical with 'set -e' since without pipefail, failures in the middle of a pipeline are silently ignored. It does not exit on failure (combine with set -e for that). It doesn't change buffering or pipe type.

QUESTION: What is the purpose of '.dockerignore' file?
OPTION_A: Defines which containers are not allowed to access specific directories on the host
OPTION_B: Configures files that are excluded from docker exec file browsing for security
OPTION_C: Specifies files and directories to exclude from the Docker build context preventing them from being sent to the Docker daemon
OPTION_D: Lists files that Docker should never copy between container layers for security reasons
EXPLANATION: .dockerignore works like .gitignore: it prevents specified files/directories from being included in the build context sent to the Docker daemon. This speeds up builds (less data transferred) and prevents sensitive files (like .git, local configs, secrets) from being accidentally COPY'd into images. It does not affect layers, host access, or exec operations.

QUESTION: Which command in ansible runs an ad-hoc task to ping all hosts in the inventory?
OPTION_A: ansible-playbook -m ping all
OPTION_B: ansible-adhoc ping --hosts=all
OPTION_C: ansible all --task=ping --check
OPTION_D: ansible all -m ping
EXPLANATION: 'ansible all -m ping' runs the ping module against all inventory hosts. -m specifies the module. ansible-playbook runs playbook files, not ad-hoc commands. --task is not a valid ansible flag. ansible-adhoc is not a valid command.

QUESTION: What does 'docker build -t myapp:v1 .' do?
OPTION_A: Rebuilds all containers using the myapp:v1 image in the current docker-compose project
OPTION_B: Pulls the myapp image version 1 from Docker Hub and builds containers from it
OPTION_C: Creates a new Docker volume named myapp and initializes it with version 1 configuration
OPTION_D: Builds a Docker image from the Dockerfile in the current directory and tags it as myapp:v1
EXPLANATION: docker build creates an image from a Dockerfile. -t tags it with name:tag. The '.' specifies the build context (current directory where Dockerfile is). It does not pull images (that's docker pull). It does not create volumes. It does not interact with docker-compose.

QUESTION: What is a 'heredoc' in bash and what is it used for?
OPTION_A: A multi-line string passed as stdin to a command using the << DELIMITER syntax commonly used for writing multi-line files or input
OPTION_B: A documentation string embedded in a bash script that appears in man page output
OPTION_C: A special bash function that inherits all variables from the parent shell without subshell isolation
OPTION_D: A bash feature that reads script content from a URL using HTTP for remote script execution
EXPLANATION: Heredoc syntax: 'cat << EOF' ... 'EOF' passes the intervening text as stdin. Used to: write multi-line files (cat << EOF > file.txt), pass multi-line SQL, configure tools needing stdin. Not related to variable inheritance (that's using dot/source). Not embedded documentation. Not URL-based execution (that's curl | bash).

QUESTION: What does 'kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml' do?
OPTION_A: Deploys the application only if no existing deployment with that name exists
OPTION_B: Validates the YAML syntax and reports errors without making changes to the cluster
OPTION_C: Applies a security policy from the YAML file to all existing deployments in the cluster
OPTION_D: Creates or updates Kubernetes resources defined in the YAML file using the declarative configuration approach
EXPLANATION: kubectl apply is the declarative approach: if the resource doesn't exist, create it; if it does exist, update it to match the YAML. This is idempotent. kubectl create fails if the resource already exists. To validate without applying, use --dry-run=client. kubectl apply always applies changes even to existing resources.

QUESTION: In a bash script, what does 'local var=value' accomplish?
OPTION_A: Exports the variable to child processes while keeping it local to the current function
OPTION_B: Creates a read-only variable that cannot be modified after declaration within the script
OPTION_C: Declares a variable that is accessible across all functions in the current script file
OPTION_D: Declares a variable that is scoped to the function where it is declared preventing it from affecting the global shell environment
EXPLANATION: local restricts variable scope to the current function (and functions called from it). Without local, variables are global to the shell script. 'local' does NOT make them readonly (use 'local -r' or 'readonly'). local variables are NOT exported to child processes. They are NOT accessible in other functions at the same level.

QUESTION: What does 'ansible-playbook site.yml --check' do?
OPTION_A: Validates the YAML syntax of the playbook file without connecting to any managed hosts
OPTION_B: Checks the connectivity to all hosts in inventory before running the playbook tasks
OPTION_C: Runs only the tasks tagged with 'check' in the playbook skipping all other tasks
OPTION_D: Runs the playbook in dry-run mode simulating what changes would be made without actually making them
EXPLANATION: --check is ansible's dry-run mode: it goes through all the motions of running the playbook (connects to hosts, gathers facts) but doesn't make actual changes. Some modules don't fully support check mode. Syntax checking uses --syntax-check. Connectivity testing uses ansible all -m ping. Selecting tags uses --tags.

QUESTION: What is the purpose of 'WORKDIR /app' in a Dockerfile?
OPTION_A: Creates the /app directory and sets it as the home directory for the container user
OPTION_B: Mounts the host's /app directory into the container as the primary working directory
OPTION_C: Sets the working directory for subsequent RUN CMD ENTRYPOINT COPY and ADD instructions in the Dockerfile
OPTION_D: Restricts all container filesystem operations to the /app directory for security isolation
EXPLANATION: WORKDIR sets the working directory for instructions that follow it in the Dockerfile. If it doesn't exist, it's created. It affects RUN, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, COPY, ADD commands. It does NOT mount host directories (that's docker run -v). It does NOT restrict filesystem access (that's security policies). It does NOT set the user home directory (that's USER and the home directory in /etc/passwd).

QUESTION: What does 'grep -v pattern file.txt' output?
OPTION_A: All lines in file.txt that do NOT match the pattern
OPTION_B: Lines matching the pattern with the matching portion removed
OPTION_C: The count of lines that do not contain the pattern
OPTION_D: Only lines where the pattern matches at the very beginning of the line
EXPLANATION: -v inverts the match: outputs lines that do NOT contain the pattern. Without -v, grep outputs matching lines. To match only at line start, use '^pattern'. To remove the matched portion, use sed. To count non-matching lines, combine with wc -l.

QUESTION: What does 'awk '{sum += $2} END {print sum}' data.txt' calculate?
OPTION_A: The count of lines where the second field is non-zero printed at the end of the file
OPTION_B: The sum of the second and following fields on each line printed after each row is processed
OPTION_C: The sum of all values in the second column of data.txt printed once after processing all lines
OPTION_D: The average of the second column calculated by summing and dividing in the END block
EXPLANATION: awk processes each line: $2 is the second field. sum += $2 accumulates. END block runs after all lines are processed — here it prints the total sum. It doesn't sum multiple fields per line (that would be $2+$3+...). It doesn't count lines. It calculates sum, not average (would need END {print sum/NR} for average).

QUESTION: In Kubernetes, what does a 'ConfigMap' store?
OPTION_A: Non-sensitive configuration data such as application settings environment variables and configuration files that can be injected into pods
OPTION_B: Encrypted sensitive data like passwords and API keys for secure application access
OPTION_C: Cluster-wide configuration for the Kubernetes control plane components
OPTION_D: The Docker image pull credentials needed for private container registry authentication
EXPLANATION: ConfigMaps store non-secret configuration: key-value pairs, configuration files, environment variable values. They can be mounted as volumes or used as env vars in pods. Private registry credentials are stored in Secrets with docker-registry type. Control plane config is in /etc/kubernetes/. Sensitive data belongs in Secrets (with encryption at rest).

QUESTION: What does 'curl -o /tmp/file.tar.gz https://example.com/file.tar.gz' do?
OPTION_A: Compresses /tmp/file.tar.gz using gzip and uploads it to the specified URL
OPTION_B: Opens the URL in a browser and saves the rendered HTML to /tmp/file.tar.gz
OPTION_C: Downloads the file and automatically extracts it to /tmp/ based on the .tar.gz extension
OPTION_D: Downloads the file from the URL and saves it to /tmp/file.tar.gz on the local filesystem
EXPLANATION: -o specifies the output filename for curl. It downloads the URL content to the local file. curl does not compress files, upload content (that uses -T or --data), render HTML, or extract archives. To extract, you'd pipe to tar: 'curl https://... | tar xz -C /tmp/'

QUESTION: A server shows high memory usage but no single process appears to be consuming excessive RAM. What should be checked?
OPTION_A: Check CPU cache size since CPU cache appears as memory usage in free and top output
OPTION_B: Shared memory usage with 'ipcs -m' memory-mapped files and kernel slab cache using 'slabtop'
OPTION_C: Run 'free -h' and if buffers exceed 1GB restart the buffer daemon service
OPTION_D: Increase the swap space since high memory usage always indicates insufficient swap
EXPLANATION: Memory that isn't attributed to individual processes may be: shared memory (ipcs -m shows System V shared memory), memory-mapped files, or kernel slab cache (slabtop shows kernel memory allocation). 'free -h' shows buffers/cache which Linux uses as disk cache (freeable). There is no 'buffer daemon'. High memory usage doesn't necessarily require more swap — Linux caches aggressively. CPU cache is not shown as memory in free/top.

QUESTION: After a power failure a filesystem check is required. 'fsck /dev/sda1' returns exit code 4. What does this mean?
OPTION_A: Filesystem errors were left uncorrected and the filesystem may not be mountable
OPTION_B: The filesystem check completed successfully with no errors found
OPTION_C: Errors were found and corrected but a reboot is required to verify
OPTION_D: The device /dev/sda1 was not found and the filesystem check could not start
EXPLANATION: fsck exit codes: 0=no errors, 1=corrected without reboot, 2=corrected, reboot needed, 4=errors left uncorrected, 8=operational error, 16=usage/syntax error, 32=canceled by user, 128=library error. Exit code 4 means errors were found but NOT fixed — the filesystem may be unmountable or inconsistent. Run 'fsck -y /dev/sda1' (unmounted) to auto-correct.

QUESTION: A service fails with 'Address already in use' when trying to start. Which command identifies which process is using the port?
OPTION_A: netstat --port PORT --identify
OPTION_B: ss -tlnp | grep :PORT or lsof -i :PORT
OPTION_C: fuser --address PORT/tcp
OPTION_D: ps aux | grep PORT
EXPLANATION: ss -tlnp shows listening TCP sockets with process info. grep :PORT filters for the specific port. lsof -i :PORT also shows what's using the port. netstat --port is not valid syntax. fuser PORT/tcp correctly identifies the PID using a TCP port (valid command). ps aux | grep PORT would only find processes with PORT in their command line arguments, not actually using the port.

QUESTION: A user's SSH key authentication is failing even though they have added their public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. What is the MOST common cause?
OPTION_A: The user needs to run 'ssh-add' to add their key to the agent before authentication works
OPTION_B: The user's shell is set to /sbin/nologin preventing key authentication from completing
OPTION_C: The SSH public key format is RSA while the server only accepts ECDSA keys
OPTION_D: Incorrect permissions on ~/.ssh directory (should be 700) or ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (should be 600)
EXPLANATION: SSH is very strict about permissions: ~/.ssh must be 700 (no group/other write), authorized_keys must be 600. If permissions are wrong, sshd ignores the authorized_keys file entirely. /sbin/nologin prevents any login (not key-specific). RSA keys are widely accepted unless explicitly disabled. ssh-add loads keys into the agent for agent forwarding but is not required for direct key auth.

QUESTION: A disk shows SMART errors 'Reallocated_Sector_Ct > 0'. What does this indicate?
OPTION_A: Normal disk behavior where sectors are optimized for performance by being relocated
OPTION_B: The partition table has been modified and sectors have been moved to new locations
OPTION_C: A filesystem error has corrupted sector allocation tables requiring fsck repair
OPTION_D: The drive has found bad sectors and remapped data to spare sectors indicating physical drive degradation
EXPLANATION: Reallocated_Sector_Ct counts sectors that failed and were remapped to spare sectors. Any non-zero value indicates physical media defects. This is a serious warning sign — the drive is failing. Replace the drive soon. This is NOT a filesystem error (fsck repairs filesystem structures, not physical defects). Partition table modifications do not generate SMART errors. There is no performance-based sector relocation in SMART terms.

QUESTION: A system boots to emergency mode with 'You are in emergency mode'. What should the administrator do first?
OPTION_A: Run 'systemctl reset-failed' to clear all failed units and boot normally
OPTION_B: Immediately reinstall the operating system since emergency mode indicates catastrophic failure
OPTION_C: Type 'exit' to attempt to continue booting past the emergency mode stage
OPTION_D: Check 'journalctl -xb' to see the boot logs and identify the unit or filesystem causing the emergency
EXPLANATION: Emergency mode: something failed critically during boot. journalctl -xb (or -xe for the current boot) shows what failed with detailed context. This helps identify: mount failures, service failures, filesystem errors. 'systemctl reset-failed' clears failed status but doesn't fix underlying issues. 'exit' in emergency mode may attempt to continue but without fixing the root cause. Emergency mode is often a filesystem mount failure, not catastrophic OS failure.

QUESTION: Which command tests if a specific kernel module can be loaded without actually loading it?
OPTION_A: lsmod --verify module_name
OPTION_B: modprobe --dry-run module_name
OPTION_C: modinfo --loadable module_name
OPTION_D: insmod --test module_name.ko
EXPLANATION: modprobe --dry-run (or -n) simulates loading a module without actually loading it. Useful for checking dependencies and seeing what would happen. insmod --test is not a valid flag for insmod. lsmod shows loaded modules but doesn't verify if an unloaded one can be loaded. modinfo shows module information but not loadability.

QUESTION: A system has 'too many open files' errors. Which command shows the system-wide and per-process file descriptor limits?
OPTION_A: proc --fd-limits shows both system and process limits in one command
OPTION_B: lsof --limits shows all current file descriptor limits system-wide
OPTION_C: sysctl -a | grep open-files shows all open file count limits
OPTION_D: cat /proc/sys/fs/file-max for system limit and ulimit -n for process limit
EXPLANATION: /proc/sys/fs/file-max is the system-wide maximum total open files (not per process). ulimit -n shows the soft limit for the current process (hard limit with -Hn). For per-process limits: /proc/PID/limits. lsof --limits is not valid. sysctl fs.file-max shows the system limit but not per-process. proc is not a user command.

QUESTION: A network connection drops frequently at random intervals. Which tool captures network packets to diagnose intermittent connectivity issues?
OPTION_A: ping -c 1000 gateway_ip to track packet loss over time
OPTION_B: mtr --report gateway_ip to identify the network hop causing drops
OPTION_C: tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/capture.pcap and analyze with Wireshark
OPTION_D: iperf3 -s on server and iperf3 -c server_ip on client for bandwidth testing
EXPLANATION: tcpdump captures raw packets to a pcap file for later analysis in Wireshark. This captures the exact packets during drops to diagnose the cause. ping shows packet loss at the IP level but not the details. mtr (Matthew's traceroute) is excellent for identifying routing issues and per-hop loss but may not capture application-level issues. iperf3 tests throughput bandwidth, not intermittent connectivity.

QUESTION: A server's clock is drifting significantly. Which command shows the current NTP synchronization status?
OPTION_A: hwclock --show-drift
OPTION_B: clockdrift --show
OPTION_C: ntpstat --verbose
OPTION_D: timedatectl status or chronyc tracking
EXPLANATION: timedatectl status shows NTP sync state and offset. chronyc tracking shows Chronyd's detailed tracking information including system time offset, RMS offset, and frequency error. ntpstat shows basic NTP status but --verbose may not be valid on all implementations. clockdrift is not a standard command. hwclock --show shows hardware clock time, not NTP drift.

QUESTION: 'df -h' shows a filesystem at 100% but you cannot find large files with 'du'. What else could be consuming space?
OPTION_A: Lost+found directory from filesystem recovery, many small files totaling large size, or open deleted files not yet freed
OPTION_B: Filesystem metadata and superblock copies are consuming all remaining space
OPTION_C: The filesystem's journal is full and needs to be truncated to free space
OPTION_D: Hidden files starting with . that du skips unless the -a flag is used
EXPLANATION: du may not show: files held open after deletion (use lsof | grep deleted), many tiny files that individually seem small but total large, and lost+found files from previous fsck. du does NOT skip hidden files — find with du -sh /dir/.* or du -ah shows them. Journal is included in filesystem usage shown by df. Filesystem metadata overhead is typically small and constant.

QUESTION: A user reports their terminal is frozen after an SSH connection interruption. How do they kill the frozen SSH session?
OPTION_A: Press Ctrl+C to send SIGINT to the SSH process which terminates it immediately
OPTION_B: Press Enter then type '~.' (tilde dot) which is the SSH escape sequence to terminate the connection
OPTION_C: Close the terminal window and open a new one since frozen SSH sessions cannot be terminated
OPTION_D: Run 'pkill ssh' from another terminal to kill all SSH processes on the system
EXPLANATION: SSH escape sequences: press Enter (to ensure it's at the start of a line) then ~ then . (dot). ~ is the default escape character. ~. terminates the connection. ~^Z suspends SSH. Ctrl+C sends SIGINT to the remote process (if connected) or may not work if the session is frozen. Closing the terminal works but loses the shell. pkill ssh kills ALL ssh connections.

QUESTION: Which command checks if a specific port is open on a remote host without nmap?
OPTION_A: telnet host port --check-only
OPTION_B: tcp-check host port
OPTION_C: ss -connect host:port
OPTION_D: bash -c 'echo >/dev/tcp/host/port' 2>/dev/null && echo open || echo closed
EXPLANATION: Bash's /dev/tcp/host/port is a special device: connecting to it attempts a TCP connection. If it succeeds (exit 0), the port is open. This uses only bash with no additional tools. telnet host port would connect (but --check-only is not valid). ss is for local socket inspection, not remote connection testing. tcp-check is not a standard command.

QUESTION: A system's /tmp directory fills up. Which command finds files in /tmp larger than 100MB?
OPTION_A: ls -lSh /tmp | head -20
OPTION_B: find /tmp -size +100M -type f
OPTION_C: du -h /tmp | sort -rh | head -20
OPTION_D: df -h /tmp --files +100M
EXPLANATION: find -size +100M finds files larger than 100MB. -type f limits to regular files. du -sh shows directory sizes (not individual large files directly). ls -lSh sorts by size and shows top 20 files (works but misses files in subdirectories). df -h /tmp --files is not valid syntax.

QUESTION: After running 'yum update' a service fails to start. The rpm database shows two conflicting package versions installed. How do you resolve this?
OPTION_A: Delete /var/lib/rpm/__db.* files and rebuild the database with 'rpm --rebuilddb'
OPTION_B: Use 'rpm -e --justdb old_package_version' to remove the old version from the database then verify with rpm -V
OPTION_C: Run 'yum clean all' which automatically removes duplicate packages from the system
OPTION_D: Use 'rpm -Fvh package.rpm' to freshen the installation and remove duplicates automatically
EXPLANATION: RPM database corruption: 'rpm -e --justdb' removes a package from the RPM database without touching files (for database-only inconsistencies). If the duplicate is actually on disk, use rpm -e package to remove it. yum clean all clears caches, not duplicates. Rebuilding the RPM database (--rebuilddb) fixes corruption but doesn't resolve actual package conflicts. rpm -F (freshen) only updates if the package is already installed.

QUESTION: A script works interactively but fails when run via cron with 'command not found'. What is the MOST likely fix?
OPTION_A: Change the script file permissions to 777 since cron requires world-executable scripts
OPTION_B: Add full paths to commands in the script or add PATH setting at the top of the crontab or script
OPTION_C: Add the user's .bash_profile to the crontab using 'source ~/.bash_profile' as first line
OPTION_D: Run the cron job as root since regular users' PATH settings don't work with cron
EXPLANATION: Cron uses a minimal environment: PATH=/usr/bin:/bin (varies by system). Commands in /usr/local/bin or /home/user/bin that work interactively may not be found. Fix: use absolute paths in scripts or set PATH explicitly in the crontab file (add 'PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin' at the top). 777 is unnecessary and a security risk. .bash_profile is for interactive shells (cron runs non-interactive). Running as root is a security risk and not necessary.

QUESTION: The command 'mount -a' fails with 'mount: wrong fs type, bad option, bad superblock on /dev/sdb1'. What is the MOST likely cause?
OPTION_A: SELinux is preventing the mount operation due to incorrect security contexts
OPTION_B: The mount point directory doesn't exist and needs to be created before mounting
OPTION_C: The filesystem type specified in fstab doesn't match the actual filesystem on the device or the device needs formatting
OPTION_D: The device /dev/sdb1 is mounted elsewhere and cannot be mounted at the specified point
EXPLANATION: 'wrong fs type, bad option, bad superblock' means: (1) fstab specifies ext4 but device has xfs (type mismatch), (2) device has never been formatted, or (3) filesystem is corrupt. Use 'blkid /dev/sdb1' to check the actual filesystem. If already mounted: 'mount | grep sdb1' or fuser. Missing mountpoint gives 'mount point does not exist'. SELinux mounting issues show different errors.

QUESTION: A process owned by a user cannot write to a directory even though 'ls -la' shows they have write permission. SELinux is disabled. What else could cause this?
OPTION_A: The user's group quota has been exceeded preventing any new file creation
OPTION_B: The directory is on an NFS mount with squash_root enabled preventing writes
OPTION_C: The user's shell is set to a restricted shell preventing file system writes
OPTION_D: A POSIX ACL denying write access to that specific user overrides the basic permission
EXPLANATION: When basic Unix permissions look correct but access is denied and SELinux is off: check ACLs with 'getfacl /path'. A DENY ACL entry for the specific user overrides the basic permissions. Group disk quota would show a quota-exceeded message. root_squash on NFS affects root, not regular users. Restricted shells limit commands, not filesystem writes in general.

QUESTION: Kernel messages show 'BUG: soft lockup - CPU#0 stuck for 22s!'. What does this indicate?
OPTION_A: The system has been running for more than 22 seconds and needs to be rebooted for updates
OPTION_B: A kernel thread or driver is holding the CPU without yielding for longer than the watchdog timer threshold
OPTION_C: The CPU has overheated and throttled to below its normal operating frequency
OPTION_D: A runaway process is consuming 100% CPU and the OOM killer has not yet terminated it
EXPLANATION: Soft lockup: the kernel watchdog detects that a CPU is not responding to scheduling for more than the threshold (usually 20 seconds). Causes: a kernel thread or device driver in a tight loop without calling schedule(), spinlock contention, or hardware issues. It is NOT about system uptime. CPU thermal throttling shows in different messages. OOM killer handles memory issues, not CPU scheduling lockups.

QUESTION: A container fails to start with 'OCI runtime exec failed: exec: exec not found'. What is the MOST likely cause?
OPTION_A: The container runtime (Docker/Podman) is not installed or the daemon is not running
OPTION_B: The user running Docker does not have permission to execute the specified container
OPTION_C: The container image was built for a different CPU architecture than the host system
OPTION_D: The executable specified in CMD or ENTRYPOINT does not exist at that path inside the container image
EXPLANATION: 'exec: exec not found' means the shell or binary specified in CMD/ENTRYPOINT does not exist inside the image at the specified path. Common: ENTRYPOINT ['/bin/bash'] but the image uses alpine which has /bin/sh not /bin/bash. Fix: use the correct binary path or ensure it's installed. If Docker wasn't running, you'd get a different daemon connection error. Architecture mismatch gives 'exec format error'. Permission issues give different errors.

QUESTION: An administrator notices that 'dmesg' shows OOM (Out of Memory) killer events. The system has free swap space. Why might OOM trigger with available swap?
OPTION_A: Swap space cannot be used by the OOM killer which only considers physical RAM
OPTION_B: The process or cgroup may have memory limits set via cgroups that prevent using swap or the kernel may be configured to not use swap via vm.swappiness=0
OPTION_C: Swap space is reserved for kernel processes and not available to user applications
OPTION_D: The OOM killer activates at 90% physical RAM usage regardless of swap availability
EXPLANATION: OOM can trigger with swap available when: (1) cgroup memory limits restrict the process to a memory limit that excludes swap, (2) vm.swappiness=0 discourages swap use so the OOM killer fires before using swap, (3) the memory zone (ZONE_DMA/ZONE_DMA32) is exhausted even if total memory is available. Swap is very much available to the OOM killer. The OOM killer has a complex scoring algorithm, not a fixed 90% threshold. Swap is for user processes, not just kernel.

QUESTION: Which log file contains information about successful and failed sudo commands?
OPTION_A: /var/log/syslog with severity level 'notice' filtering for sudo events
OPTION_B: /var/log/sudo.log which is created automatically by the sudo daemon
OPTION_C: /root/.sudo_history which logs all root commands regardless of how they were executed
OPTION_D: /var/log/auth.log (Debian/Ubuntu) or /var/log/secure (RHEL/CentOS)
EXPLANATION: sudo logs to syslog with facility 'auth' or 'authpriv'. Debian/Ubuntu writes this to /var/log/auth.log. RHEL/CentOS writes to /var/log/secure. /var/log/sudo.log is a configurable location but not created automatically. /root/.sudo_history does not exist. syslog does receive sudo messages but they go to auth.log/secure by rsyslog configuration, not directly to /var/log/syslog.

QUESTION: A server has high 'si' and 'so' values in vmstat output. What does this indicate?
OPTION_A: Socket input (si) and socket output (so) indicate excessive network connection activity
OPTION_B: Network send (si) and receive (so) packet rates are high indicating a bandwidth issue
OPTION_C: High swap-in (si) and swap-out (so) values indicate the system is actively paging memory to and from swap space suggesting RAM pressure
OPTION_D: System interrupts (si) and software interrupts (so) are consuming excessive CPU time
EXPLANATION: In vmstat: si = swap-in (pages read from swap into RAM), so = swap-out (pages written from RAM to swap). High values mean the system is actively using swap due to RAM pressure. This causes performance degradation (disk I/O for memory). bi/bo are block I/O. in/cs are interrupts/context switches. vmstat doesn't directly show network packet rates (use sar -n DEV).

QUESTION: What does 'iotop -ao' display?
OPTION_A: An aggregated overview of total system I/O by disk device without per-process breakdown
OPTION_B: Active connections sorted by I/O priority ordered from highest to lowest scheduling class
OPTION_C: All processes sorted by network output (ao = all output) with real-time bandwidth consumption
OPTION_D: Processes that have performed any disk I/O since iotop started with accumulated totals in order of most I/O
EXPLANATION: iotop: monitors disk I/O per process. -a (accumulated) shows total I/O since iotop started instead of current rate. -o (only) shows only processes that have performed I/O (hides idle processes). Combined: processes with any I/O, accumulated totals. iotop shows disk I/O, not network. It shows per-process, not just device totals. I/O priority ordering uses -p flag differently.

QUESTION: What does 'pvdisplay' show in an LVM environment?
OPTION_A: The current partition table layout for all physical disks on the system
OPTION_B: Detailed information about physical volumes including PV size PE size free PEs and the volume group it belongs to
OPTION_C: The SMART health status of all physical disks configured as LVM physical volumes
OPTION_D: Physical volume throughput statistics including read and write rates per second
EXPLANATION: pvdisplay shows LVM physical volume metadata: PV name, VG name, PV size, PE size (physical extent size), total PEs, free PEs, allocated PEs. pvs gives a compact view. This is not partition table info (fdisk/parted). Not I/O statistics (iostat). Not SMART data (smartctl).

QUESTION: What does 'dracut --force' do on a RHEL-based system?
OPTION_A: Forces dracut to include all available kernel modules regardless of what hardware is detected
OPTION_B: Regenerates the initramfs image for the currently running kernel overwriting the existing one
OPTION_C: Removes and reinstalls all dracut modules to fix a corrupted initramfs environment
OPTION_D: Forces an immediate reboot into the dracut emergency shell for system repair
EXPLANATION: dracut builds the initramfs. --force overwrites an existing initramfs file (without it, dracut refuses to overwrite). Used after kernel updates, driver changes, or when the initramfs is corrupt. It does not reboot the system. It regenerates the image but doesn't reinstall dracut itself. Without --hostonly, it includes many modules; with --hostonly, only what's needed.

QUESTION: Which command displays the current kernel boot parameters?
OPTION_A: cat /proc/cmdline
OPTION_B: dmesg | grep 'command line'
OPTION_C: uname -a --cmdline
OPTION_D: grub2-get-default --params
EXPLANATION: /proc/cmdline contains the exact kernel command line parameters used for the current boot. grub2-get-default shows the default menu entry, not parameters. uname -a shows kernel version and architecture, not boot params. dmesg does show the command line early in output but /proc/cmdline is the direct source.

QUESTION: An administrator needs to change a user's primary group to 'developers'. Which command is correct?
OPTION_A: groupmod --primary developers username
OPTION_B: usermod -G developers username
OPTION_C: chgrp developers /home/username
OPTION_D: usermod -g developers username
EXPLANATION: usermod -g (lowercase) changes the primary group. usermod -G (uppercase) sets the supplementary groups list (would REPLACE all supplementary groups). chgrp changes file ownership, not user group settings. groupmod modifies group properties like name or GID, not user membership.

QUESTION: What is the purpose of 'tune2fs -c 30 /dev/sdb1'?
OPTION_A: Changes the ext filesystem block size to 30 kilobytes for improved large file performance
OPTION_B: Configures the filesystem to use 30 percent of space as reserved for root operations
OPTION_C: Sets a 30-day interval between mandatory filesystem consistency checks
OPTION_D: Sets the maximum number of mounts before a forced filesystem check to 30 on an ext filesystem
EXPLANATION: tune2fs -c sets the maximum mount count before fsck is forced. -c 30 means fsck runs after 30 mounts. -i sets the time interval (use -i 30d for 30 days). Block size is set at mkfs time and cannot be changed with tune2fs. Reserved blocks percentage uses -m (e.g., -m 5 for 5%).

QUESTION: What does 'mount --bind /source /destination' do?
OPTION_A: Creates a union mount combining the contents of both directories at /destination
OPTION_B: Makes /source accessible at /destination as a bind mount without creating a separate filesystem
OPTION_C: Creates a hard link between two mount points sharing the same inode table
OPTION_D: Copies all files from /source to /destination and keeps them synchronized
EXPLANATION: Bind mounts make a directory accessible at another path — same filesystem, same files, same inodes. Changes in either location are visible in both. This is useful for chroot environments or exposing subdirectories at different paths. Not a hard link (those are per-file). Not a copy (rsync/cp). Not a union mount (use overlayfs for that).

QUESTION: Which systemd target is equivalent to runlevel 3 (multi-user text mode with network)?
OPTION_A: basic.target
OPTION_B: runlevel3.target
OPTION_C: network-online.target
OPTION_D: multi-user.target
EXPLANATION: Systemd target equivalents: runlevel 0=poweroff.target, 1=rescue.target, 3=multi-user.target, 5=graphical.target, 6=reboot.target. runlevel3.target is a compatibility symlink pointing to multi-user.target. network-online.target ensures network is up but is not equivalent to a runlevel. basic.target is a dependency target, not a runlevel equivalent.

QUESTION: What does 'alternatives --config python' do on a RHEL/CentOS system?
OPTION_A: Automatically sets the highest installed Python version as the system default
OPTION_B: Updates the Python package and all its dependencies to the latest available version
OPTION_C: Shows all files and symlinks associated with the current default Python installation
OPTION_D: Presents an interactive menu to choose which Python version is used as the default 'python' command
EXPLANATION: alternatives (similar to update-alternatives on Debian) manages symlinks for commands with multiple versions. --config presents an interactive selection menu. It does not auto-select or update packages. To list (not interactively configure), use 'alternatives --list'. '--display python' shows current status and alternatives.

QUESTION: What is the purpose of '/etc/skel/' directory?
OPTION_A: Holds template configuration files for the package manager's initial repository setup
OPTION_B: Stores skeleton boot configuration files used as templates for new system services
OPTION_C: Contains template files that are copied to every new user's home directory when the account is created
OPTION_D: Contains minimal rescue system files used when booting into single-user emergency mode
EXPLANATION: /etc/skel/ (skeleton): useradd copies its contents to new home directories. Typical contents: .bashrc, .bash_profile, .profile. Admins add files here to provide default configurations for all new users. Not related to boot, emergency mode, or package management.

QUESTION: Which command shows memory usage broken down by application including shared memory correctly attributed?
OPTION_A: top -b -n 1 -o %MEM
OPTION_B: smem -t -k
OPTION_C: ps aux --sort=-%mem | head -20
OPTION_D: free -h --detail
EXPLANATION: smem provides accurate memory reporting: PSS (Proportional Set Size) attributes shared memory proportionally. This gives a more accurate view than RSS (Resident Set Size) which counts shared memory fully for each process. free -h doesn't break down by application. ps aux shows RSS which overcounts shared memory. top also uses RSS/VIRT which can be misleading.

QUESTION: An administrator needs to configure GRUB2 to boot the previous kernel by default. Which steps are correct?
OPTION_A: Set GRUB_DEFAULT=previous in /etc/default/grub and run 'systemctl restart grub2'
OPTION_B: Run 'grub2-set-default previous' and then 'grub2-install /dev/sda'
OPTION_C: Edit /boot/grub2/grub.cfg directly changing the default entry number and save the file
OPTION_D: Edit /etc/default/grub setting GRUB_DEFAULT to the entry number or 'saved', run grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg
EXPLANATION: GRUB2 configuration: edit /etc/default/grub (user-friendly config), then regenerate /boot/grub2/grub.cfg with grub2-mkconfig. Never edit grub.cfg directly — it's regenerated and changes are lost. 'grub2-set-default previous' is not valid (use grub2-set-default 0 or grub2-set-default 'menuentry title'). grub2-install installs the bootloader to MBR/EFI, not needed just to change default. systemctl doesn't restart grub2.

QUESTION: What does 'nohup command &' accomplish?
OPTION_A: Runs the command without any output going to the terminal by redirecting to /dev/null
OPTION_B: Runs the command with no CPU or memory limits in the background for maximum performance
OPTION_C: Runs the command in the background immune to the SIGHUP signal so it continues running after the terminal closes
OPTION_D: Starts the command as a system service that survives reboots in the background
EXPLANATION: nohup: prevents the SIGHUP signal (sent when terminal closes) from terminating the process. & puts it in the background. Output goes to nohup.out by default (not /dev/null).
